body_markdown:
There was a time, not all that long ago, that Nissan’s fourth-generation Z-car was a sexy, common sight on U.S. roads. The carmaker sold nearly 90,000 copies of the Z32 300ZX between 1990 and ’96, and these included 222-horsepower normally aspirated T-top coupes and 2+2s, along with an eventual convertible. King of the hill, however, was the 300-hp twin-turbocharged two-seater, a car that easily went toe to toe not just with its Japanese rivals from Toyota and Mazda, but with the[C4 Corvette](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/chevrolet/corvette/1991/1991-chevrolet-corvette-base?id=aCn1I000000DOBqSAO) and[Porsche 944](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=porsche+944) .


These days, they are a much rarer sight. They spent a great many years in the “used car” realm, and many were chewed up and spit out by a series of overzealous and/or underfunded owners. In the meantime, there have also been three subsequent Z-car generations. Every so often, however, we seem to encounter an exemplary Z32, and that was very much the case this week in Dallas, when Mecum sold[this 17,000-mile example](https://www.mecum.com/lots/1181112/1990-nissan-300zx-turbo/) for $64,350. It’s not a record, but it is big money for a car that certainly deserved it.


Mecum

Datsun (Nissan’s export brand of the day) stunned the world in 1969 with the introduction of the[240Z](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=datsun+240z) , the gorgeous little coupe that brought reliable performance to the masses. The malaise-y regulatory milieu that followed afflicted enthusiast and commuter cars far and wide, including the second-gen S130[280ZX](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=datsun+280zx) and first-gen[(Z31) 300ZX](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/datsun/300zx/1984/1984-datsun-300zx-turbo?id=aCn1I000000CuphSAC) , despite Nissan’s best efforts keep them exciting. By the end of the 1980s, however, fans of the badge were ready to be wowed once again. And boy, did Nissan deliver.


Based on development and refinement of a mid–1980s concept car called the Mid4, Nissan applied much of what it learned directly to the Z32, which was being developed in parallel. Crucially, this included the Z’s Super High Capacity Actively Controlled Suspension, or HICAS, which allowed for four-wheel steering and impressively athletic movement. The 3.0-liter, twin-turbocharged VG30DETT V-6 engine, too, came out of the concept car. When paired with the five-speed manual, its 300 horses at 6400 rpm and 283 lb-ft of torque at 3600 rpm were enough to propel the Z to 60 mph in 5.5 seconds, with a top speed of 153 mph.


The Z’s shapely design, meanwhile, with steeply raked headlights incorporated into the sharp nose, gave the car a 0.31 drag coefficient, which made it more slippery than the Porsches, Corvettes, and Supra Turbos it was aimed at. To finish things off, drivers were treated to an interior that enveloped them, “perhaps the most beautiful and efficient cockpit in the sports-car kingdom,” wrote Arthur St. Antoine in the August 1989 issue of *Car and Driver* . “Trust us,” he continued, “sports-car cockpits don’t get any better than this.”


Mecum


And in 2026, few 300ZXs get any better than *this* . Of the 39,104 Zs built in their debut year, the rarest color was Gold Pearl (1200 cars) and then Yellow Pearlglow (1225, 1.7% of production), the hue on this car. It’s a stunning color, too, and such a wonderful departure from the reds (7687 in Aztec Red) and blacks (7264 in Diamond Black Pearl) that seem so prevalent on these cars.


The car was not perfect; with nearly 17,000 miles on the clock, it couldn’t be. There are some scuffs to the front valance; the “NISSAN” and “TWIN TURBO” labels beneath the rear spoiler appear to have peeled away; and the steering wheel, shifter, and driver’s seat show some light wear. The car was driven, after all. But it is a solid car in the condition[#2 (excellent)](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/nissan/300zx/1990/1990-nissan-300zx-turbo?id=aCn1I000000CxBqSAK&condition=excellent) range. On the day, it sold for low condition #1 (concours) money. Potato, potahto. If you were in the market for a stellar Z from what is arguably Nissan’s peak era, you’d be waiting a long time for another this nice to come around. And if you wanted a faster, more sophisticated Z for much less, you could have bid on[the 370Z](https://www.mecum.com/lots/1180093/2009-nissan-370z/) offered 62 lots later, which was a no-sale at $11,000.

A handful of Z32s have sold for more in the last two years, including[a red, one-owner 9800-mile car](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/past-sales/1991-nissan-300zx/JN1CZ24H6MX500520/3334439e-b610-4c37-800a-097409ef9c76) at Barrett-Jackson Scottsdale for $73,700, a rare[Steve Millen–modified SMZ](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/past-sales/1995-nissan-300zx/JN1CZ24D6SX570366/19ca15ae-7e8c-4259-8066-74300389a3b9) in black for $90,300, and the current tracked high sale, at $91,350,[a black ’91 with 6900 miles](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/past-sales/1991-nissan-300zx/JN1CZ24H9MX502178/a5324da7-d5fd-4960-b8e6-947f96d5178d) sold last spring by Cars & Bids for $91,350.


None of those Zs was a true concours example, either, frankly. They were very nice, certainly, and also far more common colors. In Dallas, the consignor off-loaded a terrific, eye-catching Z for big money, but the buyer didn’t overpay. Everybody won here.
